utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask you, please, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Michael McVicker and assisted by Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. And for the Defence in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. John Ostojic on behalf of Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I learned that the videolink in the moment is not yet stable. May I ask the audio and video unit -- I can see -- it's okay?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we can start immediately. Hello, Madam Dahuron. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Unfortunately, we can't hear you. Could you please speak some words.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, better. Can everybody hear Madam Dahuron? It's okay. May I ask for the appearances in Banja Luka, who is please present in Banja Luka in the room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] At this moment, there is only audio/visual unit and myself. Witness is waiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Today we have two cameras, one covering the entire room, and one specially for the witness. May I ask before we start, Mr. Ostojic, any protective measures you would need in addition?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: None that I am aware of, Your Honour, but perhaps we can inquire directly of the witness just to be certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in Banja Luka in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you before we start, do you regard it necessary that we have protective measures especially designed for you, or may it be in open court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need any protective measures. Whatever I have to say, I can say it publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. You are called as a Defence witness, and therefore, may I ask Defence counsel to start with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Becner. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am glad to be able to contribute to the perception -- to establishing the perception and the views of my acquaintance, Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to ask you a couple of questions, and I would ask that you please allow me to complete the question before you give us your response. And also, if you do not understand the question, please affirmatively state that you do not understand it and ask for clarification at which point I'll be more than happy to clarify any questions we put to you. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, sir, can you please state your full name, first and last name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Becner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Becner, can you please share with us a little bit about your personal background. Can you tell us where you currently reside and with whom.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I currently reside in Prijedor in Srpskih Velikana Street Number 323. I have a Ph.D. in economics. I work as a full-time professor at the management school in Prijedor, and I also work as a professor and a member of the faculty and business in Novi Sad. I am married. I have two children, and I am happy to say that I also have three grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Wonderful. Sir, can you tell us the year in which you received your Ph.D. in economics.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I received my Ph.D. in economics in the year 2000 from the university in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us briefly your employment -- your current employment status. Can you tell us in the last 10 to 15 years, if you will, where were you employed and in what capacity did you hold such employment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Throughout my professional career, I worked in different walks of life, and I worked in various capacities. I was the secretary-general of the school of music in Prijedor. I was also the head of tourist and transport office of the ZTP Sarajevo, the branch office in Prijedor. I was also the director of the driving school in Prijedor. That was I immediately up to the beginning of the war, then I also owned my own driving school, Zolka, in Prijedor. Since 1994, I have been the founder and one of the professors of the business management school in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, forgive me for asking this question, but can you share with us what your ethnic background is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I was born in a mixed marriage. My father is a German and my mother is a Croat. But I have declared myself as a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, had you declared yourself as a Croat also in 1992 as such?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: This is what was written in all the documents. This is not how I declared myself as, but this is what was registered, what has been registered in all of my documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Moving right long, if I may, sir, can you tell me about the general situation in northwest Bosnia, and specifically in Prijedor, during the period of the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: During that period of time, I had my own business, and I was in the education. I didn't -- I was not involved in politics. But everybody could notice that the situation was very tense and that the tension arose from ethnic issues. I belonged to the type of people who have made everything in the former Yugoslavia, and therefore supported the former Yugoslavia. However, the situation developed in a different direction as everybody could see at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I may ask in part a leading question of you, were you ever involved or participated in the sales of hunting guns or weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: When I was giving information about my profession, I omitted to say - not on purpose - that at the same time when I had the driving school, I also had a retail store which was registered, amongst other things, for the sale of ammunition and hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, sir, was that during the period of the spring and summer of 1992, both before and after? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Let me clarify. That retail store was open up to May 1992 immediately before the first conflict. At that time, none of the retail stores were open any longer, so mine was not an exception to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can take you back to those ten and a half-plus years, the period immediately before you shut down your retail store, was there an increase in the sales of such hunting guns, weapons, and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: There was no increase, although the demand was somewhat higher. However, the -- our sources of supply, that was the Zastava from Kragujevac, we had a contract with them, and there were other colleagues of mine in other towns who were engaged in the same kind of job. And the quotas of weapons that we received was the same. My store was little. It was some 3 and a half kilometres away from the town, and it was my friends, the hunters, who used my services most because let me remind you, I graduated from the school of economics. I also received my masters degree, and I received my Ph.D. all with the same subject matter, and that was hunting and hunting economy. And therefore, this was a logical development, that my colleagues would go to my store to ask for my services.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just describe for us, if you will, the type of weapons and armaments that you sold and the use of those weapons on what type of animals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: This was all hunting weapons, hunting rifles, and hunting shotguns as well as the ammunitions for the same types of weapons. And those weapons were used for the small animals and for the big animals alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn to something that you stated initially when you appeared, that you're an acquaintance of Dr. Stakic. Can you share with us, sir, how you met his acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I knew Dr. Stakic. I met him before the war. But we were just nodding acquaintances. In simple words, he was just one of the doctors in the medical centre in Prijedor. I got to know him a bit better in the year 1993 when I cooperated with his institution, and his institution was the occupational medicine in Prijedor. We made a cooperation contract, and our cooperation involved the issuing of medical certificates for all the prospective drivers. We cooperated for about a year, and our cooperation was really good. During that period of time, not for a single moment did I observe any kind of behaviour on the part of Dr. Stakic that would show me that he had ethnic prejudices. He was a very pleasant person, and he respected his family and he also respected those who cooperated with him and who worked alongside him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, at any time during the period that you knew Dr. Stakic, did he exhibit any ill will, hatred, or animosity against Muslims, Croats, or other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I would see Dr. Stakic several times every week, either in his office when we would discuss business or when we went for a drink to one of the bars in Prijedor. Not for a single moment did I notice any kind of chauvinism or ethnic animosity or any similar thing. Let me be more specific. Among many people who are my colleagues and who had their own driving schools and who were Serbs, Dr. Stakic decided to cooperate with me, and I am not a Serb. I don't know why he did that. I did not pay any attention to that. But let me say that in my presence, he never showed any signs of any ethnic animosity, hatred, or any kind of undermining people of different ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us your opinion, sir, if you feel that Dr. Stakic treated you, a Croat, a non-Serb, any differently than he treated people of the Serbian ethnic background, or were you treated the same?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: There was no difference in his behaviour. Very often, when we socialised outside his office, we would find ourselves with our colleagues and peers, and we would joke. We would talk informally. In these conversations, there was not any sign of any discrimination against me or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, if at any time during the periods that you were with Dr. Stakic you observed or recognised Dr. Stakic exercising any violent means or threats against anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I didn't notice, not for a single moment. And personally, I believe that he was a doctor and a humanitarian. Whenever we talked about that, we talked about the normal life, the standard way of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did at any time, sir, you observe from Dr. Stakic any nationalistic radical idealogy or policies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I am determined when I say no, and especially never in my presence. But I also believe that he has never displayed any such feelings in the conversations with other people. Prijedor is a small town, and nationalism cannot be hidden from people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Describe for us if you will the personal treatment you received from Dr. Stakic both in private and in public if it differed. And, sir, what I'm trying to determine, if I may, is to determine whether Dr. Stakic treated you differently when you were in public with him, in public venues, when as you say you went out and occasionally had a drink. Did he treat you any different, the same while you were in public versus private?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Let me explain. In our business contacts and in our private contacts, I always received the same treatment, and that entailed mutual respect and correctness. Very often, I would go into his office unannounced. I would sit there with him for a certain period of time. We would exchange ideas, or we would discuss business matters. I never had any problem talking to him. I was never discriminated against. I was never treated differently from anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you, sir, in your own words describe for us Dr. Stakic's character that which you have concluded with respect to his integrity, his temperament, and to his honesty.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I'm not a psychologist. I've told you that I am an economist by profession. But I'm a humanitarian, and I find it easy to recognise those people who are the same as me. I would not like to say anything bad about a different profession, but I would still like to answer your question. Dr. Stakic is a -- by the way he looks, by the way he behaves, he came across as a kind person, and he was received well by everybody. He has never imposed his views on other people, or at least I have never experienced him imposing his views on other people. So I would say that he is a quiet and a self-effacing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I have not met Dr. Becner before today, and I'm happy to meet his acquaintance, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution, the Prosecution is prepared for cross-examination immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just take five minutes, please, to review our notes and resume at around 3.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. You understood the Prosecution is prepared to put to you questions in cross-examination in about 5 minutes. Could you please wait these five minutes. I don't know whether -- what is less expensive, to have the line going on or... Would it be better to have a break? So then let's wait and stand by. If I may kindly ask you to stay there and I will call you back in 5 minutes when the Prosecution is prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've understood what you said, and it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honour wants to use this time, I could comment on the 92 bis declarations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the moment, the -- you should be aware that the witness can follow what we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that given the very general nature of my remarks, and that is simply that having reviewed those that I received today, I could give the witness numbers just to make sure that we're talking about the same numbers -- I'm sorry, they do not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have numbers. But I received the package from Your Honour. I'm sure it's the same that Your Honours received. We do not have an objection to any of these, and we are not requesting that they be brought for cross-examination. Of course, this is not to say that we accept all statements and conclusions of the witness or assertions of fact. But we do not believe it would be particularly useful to bring those witnesses here to The Hague to testify. So we would be willing from the side of the Prosecution to accept these 92 bis statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: These comments would be true for all of the seven we received today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All the seven statements. And to be quite concrete, you have no problems with the questions related to the influence of Dr. Stakic on the military, especially as to the fact that it's not extremely concrete where this mobilisation took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, we do not agree with these conclusions of these witnesses. We do note the fact Your Honour just stated as far as the lack of concreteness of some of the witnesses' assertions regarding influence given the position of these witnesses to observe or know about the relationship. As to the specifics about the mobilisation, to be frank, we would be willing -- we're not going to argue, just so Your Honours and the Defence know, that the witnesses didn't go to Dr. Stakic and he didn't say, "I can't do anything for you." But in wartime, it's very difficult especially for any political leader to simply excuse people because they are his friends from military service. And we do not -- we will assert that that does not itself that the witness did not have influence or even the ability if he so choose to exempt someone. But sons of presidents of countries serve in wartime in armed services. This is not conclusive, we believe, but we accept the facts that the witnesses went to Dr. Stakic, did ask and then received a negative response from Dr. Stakic regarding exempting these individuals from military service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, it means that the Prosecution and of course the Defence, having submitted these statements, they would be in agreement that if without any change of the wording of the statements, these statements could be accepted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it is premature to be decided now because it has not yet been signed. So we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I should say not that not all members of the Prosecution team have reviewed those statements, but those are my initial comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As to the fact that the Prosecution is one unit, we take it as the submission by the Prosecution. And I think that is okay. Any other remarks by the Defence in the moment related to the 92 bis statements? We expect the other four during the day or maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain of those four, Your Honour, but I would like to address the Court on it at some later time, perhaps this afternoon. With respect to the comments from my learned friend, we are grateful that they do not have an objection. I would just like to point out to the Court in connection with the issues of mobilisation and time of death, as the statements themselves reflect, there will be attachments to the statements as exhibits the issues that the Court and the OTP raise as to the specific date of death and the date of mobilisation. I see in this packet that was somewhat prematurely offered that those documents were not included. We reviewed them in part and they are expected to be attached to the affidavits where applicable to three if not four of the witnesses that have provided us with those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just one further caveat, we have not yet had the chance to search our database for specific information that may either corroborate or throw into dispute some of these issues, particularly about particular individuals' mobilisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe everybody in this courtroom agrees that it would be premature to finally decide on the admission of evidence before we have the signed statement with all the attachments. May I ask, what about the Prosecution starting cross-examination? You are ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Becner, you are prepared to continue with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the floor is for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Mr. Becner, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Mr. Becner, my name is Mike McVicker, and I am representing the Prosecution today. What I'd like to do right now is just take a few moments to clarify some of your testimony that you just gave. If you don't understand the question, please ask, and I will repeat it. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: I have just a few questions about your hunting rifle business. Was it only hunting rifles that you sold, or did you sell other sorts of guns or arms?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I sold only hunting rifles. As I've said, the one intended for big and small game, shotguns and rifles, hunting rifles as we call them, in hunting jargon. And in addition to that, I also sold pistols, and I was licensed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Did people from all ethnicities purchase rifles and pistols from you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. People of all ethnicities used to buy in my shop. I still have the records with me today because one copy of the purchasing permit needs to remain in my records. And this is why I have kept the records even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Did you ever provide copies of those records to Serbian government authorities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: My shop was open up until the takeover of power. And following that, following the takeover, as we already know, conflicts started breaking out. There were certain controversies, therefore there was need for people to go hunting or there was no need to procure such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Becner. But my question was: Did you personally provide Serbian government authorities in 1992 with the records of people who had purchased weapons from you before then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Following the takeover of power by the Serbian side, so to speak, the MUP of Prijedor carried out inspection of all entities selling weapons in the time period prior to that. In the course of that inspection, they also carried out the search of my house and the inspection of my records. The entire records were returned to me, and all of the weapons were left there, the ones that were not sold at the time. And those were two carbines of calibre 70.4 and 30.06.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Do you know who in the MUP from Prijedor carried out those inspections?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: There were two policemen from Prijedor MUP. I didn't know either of them, but I got to know one of them. One was Kovacevic, and his first name might have been Radovan. The information I provided I provided to a man whose first name I believe is Milisav, but I'm not sure about that. He was an inspector in the SUP in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Becner. I'd like to clarify one question concerning your ethnicity in 1992. You stated that your identification papers listed that you were a Croat, but that, as I understood it, you did not declare yourself as a Croat. So to be clear, did you declare yourself a specific ethnicity in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I have to say that when a child is born, nobody asks the child what the ethnicity is. Rather, the ethnicity is written down in the birth Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. certificate. And my ethnicity was written down in my birth certificate without anybody ever asking me what my ethnicity was. Let me clarify: I live in an environment in the village or a suburb of Prijedor inhabited by Serbs. Despite the fact that my parents were members of the Partizan movement, nobody ever gave a bad look to my family either in the past or now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: In the 1991 census, how did you declare your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to move ahead to the events around 30th of April, 1992. Were you in Prijedor on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, as I've mentioned, I was in a settlement which is 3 and a half kilometres from downtown area. At the time, it wasn't desirable for anyone to move about in the streets of the town and thereabouts. It wasn't desirable for anyone including myself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that the witness mentioned the name of the settlement but we didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Could the witness please clarify the name of the settlement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: The settlement is called Gomjenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Becner.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Before the war, there was a street called Partizanska Street there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Mr. Becner, were you engaged in any combat activity between 30 April 1992 and 30 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No, I did not -- I was not. Towards late August, or rather in early August, I was engaged in the territorial unit within the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what you mean by "engaged in the territorial unit of the local commune."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: At the time, especially after the 30th of April, in local communes, there were commissions established as a way of self-defence, and they also set up night watches or night guards along the borders of villages where -- bordering with other entity or rather entities inhabited by Muslims in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Did you personally meet or otherwise communicate with Dr. Stakic between 30th of April, 1992, and around 30th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No, never. During that period of time, it was impossible. I was in Gomjenica, and I don't know where he was and what kind of work he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: When you say -- it was well-known, wasn't it, Mr. Becner, that Dr. Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I know that Dr. Stakic was president of municipality. What office he was assigned following that, I don't know. I wasn't interested in that, nor were other people interested in that. The situation was such, at least where I lived, that people didn't care about that. My neighbours and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: During your testimony, you said that you discussed business in Dr. Stakic's office. Could you please tell me what sort of business you were discussing with him.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: The first contact pertained to establishing the share of my driving school, the share of the revenue, how much needs to be paid to the occupational medicine company and how much should be paid to physicians involved in issuing medical certificates. At the time, I dealt with managerial tasks pertaining to issuing of medical certificates, whereas the entity issuing these certificates was the occupational medicine company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss any other business with Dr. Stakic in his office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: In view of the time that has passed, it is difficult to remember all of the details of the conversation. However, what I can say -- what I should say and what I feel as a person is that these questions did not touch upon nationalism and other problems arising in connection with the situation, Prijedor and the battlefield and so on. Our conversations mostly related to business issues or other topics that would be touched upon in any normal, regular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: So your company was paying money to Dr. Stakic's occupational medical clinic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that the witness testified that there was an occupational clinic owned exclusively by Dr. Stakic, so it is somewhat presumptuous and it presumes facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic the head of the occupational medicine clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Did your company pay money to that clinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I have to clarify. We had a partnership relationship. We had a business relationship. My company was in charge of organisation, organisational matters. And therefore, from the money collected by those who sought medical certificates, we received a certain percentage. The other part related to the costs of using the premises and equipment of the occupational medicine clinic as well as remuneration for work, retirement compensation, and social security benefits for the people who worked part-time in my company after having worked in the occupational medicine clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: You also discussed in your testimony that you socialised with Dr. Stakic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Can you tell me some of the other people who were present during those occasions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: There was the late Dr. Mico Kovacevic with whom I went -- rather, Balaban Slobodan with whom I went to high school. Vaso Cvijic, director of Zitopromet company, and some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kovacevic ever display any sort of nationalistic feelings or express those feelings in your presence and in front of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No, never. Dr. Mico Kovacevic was a happy person, a pleasant person to socialise with. And at least in my presence, he never exhibited any signs of nationalism either with respect to myself or while talking to Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask only a few additional questions. Sir, do you have any other nationality than the Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I do not have two ethnicities. But whenever I introduce -- when I introduce myself, I told you that my father was a German, and that I do have some sort of a German affiliation in that respect. But in Tito's Yugoslavia, let me remind you, and especially after the establishment of Tito's Yugoslavia, it was not popular to be a German in Yugoslavia. And as my mother was a Croat, me and my siblings were registered as Croats in our birth certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. One other concretisation, please. Where did you actually live in April 1992? I have a map before me, and could you -- is it in the neighbourhood of Prijedor or what is the exact name and area where you live?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Gomjenica is the name of that neighbourhood. It is upstream of the Sana River, and Gomjenica River towards the Sanicani some 3 and a half kilometres from the city centre. At the time the name of the street was Partizanska, and currently it is Srpskih Velikana Street, and the number is still the same, it is 323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the map, I see a huge area called Gomjenica. Could you clarify a little bit more what is the town or the hamlet you lived in.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: It is on the Prijedor/Tomasica Road. That is where you will find Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this hamlet Gomjenica. You cross the bridge on the Gomjenica River, and then you go towards Tomasica, and you pass the Sanicani fish pond. That fish pond is at the far end of this settlement, Gomjenica, and almost at the end of that main road that passes through this settlement of Gomjenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever in April or May 1992 hear and/or see helicopters landing in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Gomjenica is a relatively peacefully local commune, particularly in the area where I live. At that time, there was no need for any helicopters to fly over, nor did they indeed fly over at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned "at that time." Did you see any special movements by helicopters in your area immediately -- say starting with the beginning of 1992 and until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it from your statement that you did not really socialise with Dr. Stakic before September 1992, but only met him and it was limited to a mutual nodding. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever meet the family of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You gave a long and extremely clear characterisation of the personality of Dr. Stakic. Can you please tell us what is the basis for this, your assessment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: It is a very difficult question on the face of it. And the answer would contain a moral obligation on my part. I said at the beginning that I am a humanitarian person by nature. Already in grammar school when others didn't want to jump into the Sana River, I saved two people who were drowning. I don't know their names to this very day. I also believe that it is humanitarian, that it is honest and moral to say something about the person, what one has experienced about that person. As I've already said, that's how I have seen Dr. Stakic, and that is the only way I have seen him and I have perceived him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, how often did you meet Dr. Stakic approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Two or three times a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why was this that it was necessary to meet two or three times a week?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: It was not a need or an obligation, simply twice a week, I had to attend inspections or exams. I had to sit in those exams twice a week. He would also be there, so we would have a drink after that. It was only logical that I was there and that we would have a drink after those exams afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Dr. Stakic in the building of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall the events of the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: All the people who lived in Prijedor at the time remember those events. But they -- their perceptions are from different angles, just like the place where people found themselves at the time were different. I've already told you that me and my family, that we were in Gomjenica, and that at the time the electricity was cut and there was no water, and we experienced a lot of problems every day. Before those events, there were some tensions in Prijedor, and I found that very difficult to accept. I have always been an advocate of the federation, of a weak federation at the time. But the events started going in a different direction and leading in a different direction. In that context, my influence or my contribution could be only minimum or none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How did you learn about the takeover in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Through the media, radio and television. Actually, it was on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who announced the takeover on the radio?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I have to think. One of the announcers. I can't remember if it was Senad Dzapic or Marinovic or somebody else. I can't remember. Let me tell you another thing, if I may. Like everywhere, there is also a hearsay or the grapevine on which you can hear news. And things, rumours, can be heard about different things and about different events on the grapevine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dr. Stakic on the radio or see him on television? In 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, I was a little bit surprised when previously you testified that you did not know what kind of work Dr. Stakic did, and then later: "I didn't care about what happened." Are you or have you been aware in 1992 about the investigation centres or camps or - I don't know which expression you would prefer to use?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: When I said that I was not interested in some things, maybe I have not chosen the right expression. In simple words, there was no way for me to influence things, and that's why I used this word, that I was not interested. But it is not the best expression. As far as the camps are concerned, I was never in any of the camps. And a little while ago, I said that there was a system of conveying news. How reliable that system was and how reliably it really depicted the situation, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Last question: Did you ever meet Mr. Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I met Simo Drljaca only once during the war. We greeted each other because we knew each other before the war. He learned to drive in my driving school, and so did his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You gave us some characteristics and assessment of the personalities of Dr. Stakic and others. What would be your personal impression of Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: During the period when I knew the late Simo Drljaca, he worked in the centre for primary education in Prijedor. He was a keen fisherman. And he was a pretty anonymous person in Prijedor. During the war, I did not have an opportunity to talk to him or see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I forgot to ask you. Was it possible to continue with your driving school during May to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: At that time, none of the companies worked, none of the driving schools, and mine was not an exception. It was only in 1993, in May 1993, when companies were opened again and when the economy was revived, and then my company could also continue its business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did your company stop continuing with the business, in 1992 or was it maybe already earlier, and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Immediately prior to April 1992, the socially-owned company, the Prijedor Driving School that I was the director of, pursuant to the legal regulations that were in place at the time distributed its assets to its employees who were then able to establish their own private driving schools. The law in question is the so-called Markovic's law. The driving schools that were established in such a way started operating, but there was no interest from the prospective candidates. As for the period that you mentioned, such interest died completely. Nobody actually banned the work of a driving schools or other companies for that matter, but there were no objective conditions in place for the operation of any of the companies. There were checkpoints in local communes, on the roads, so the roads were not passable. And for that reason, driving schools could not operate, and their business was not needed by the general public at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the basis for your income in the period from April through September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: At that time, nobody received income, and that included me. My wife as well. And a number of others who worked in the socially-owned companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have two questions: What were the relations between Dr. Stakic and Simo Drljaca between April 1992 to September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because I never saw them together. Therefore, I am not able to tell you what their relationship was. I can only assume that those relationships were friendly, but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between Dr. Stakic and Dr. Kovacevic in the same period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I believe the relationship was friendly, and that they were also in a sort of a business relation because Dr. Kovacevic was Dr. Stakic's superior. Dr. Kovacevic was the director of the medical centre, and Dr. Stakic was the head of the occupational medicine department. And I believe that their relationship was good, both as colleagues as well as private individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the relationship between Dr. Stakic and Dr. Kovacevic between April 30th of, 1992, and September 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I apologise. I have misunderstood your question. In that period, I was never in a position to be together with the two of them, so I can't answer. But from mid-1993 onwards, their relationship was the way I have just described it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay, please. No questions. May I ask the Defence, are there any questions in addition emanating from the line of questions put to the witness by the Prosecution or the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, John Ostojic again. I want to clarify a question that the president of our Chamber asked you, the Honourable Judge Schomburg. You testified according to the LiveNote, page 22, line 16, regarding the lack of electricity, and I think you stated "electricity was cut. There was no water." Just, sir, so that I am clear on the time period that you were referring to, is it true that the electricity was cut and there was no water in the Prijedor Municipality on May 30th, 1992, the day in which the city/town was attacked? Correct.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: I have to think. I believe that at that time there was electricity, but there were frequent cut offs. And since I live in the suburbs where the water pressure is very weak, as soon as there are some disturbances, some hiccups, we don't have water.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, if I may: You're a well-educated and obviously intelligent man. If Dr. Stakic held any nationalistic, radical views or prejudices against Croats, you would have been able to pick up on those characteristics, would you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: The way he engaged me, although there were other driving schools and other people, speaks in favour of that. And I've already told you that he did not show any signs of nationalism. In my team, there was a nurse Suada, who was a Muslim lady, and she could work there without any problems. And Dr. Stakic never made any distinction among the members of his staff. In the occupational medicine department, the climate was such that there were no signs of nationalism whatsoever. The spirit of cooperation was good in that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Additional questions by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: Just one, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: In response to the question just asked by Mr. Ostojic, that assessment is based from a time period after September 30th, 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BECNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCVICKER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it remains for me to thank you, Mr. Becner, for your testimony in Banja Luka. And you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask that, please Madam Dahuron, once again appears on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Your Honour, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to confirm for the following days that the order remains unchanged? Now, that would mean tomorrow Witness 039 for a period, estimated period of three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] That is the last information I have for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then 037, two and a half hours on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Your Honour -- indiscernible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then on Thursday, because this is a crucial date, Witness 030, for only one hour. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Your Honour, I haven't received the update. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that we are on the safe side and hear this witness with the estimated time for the examination-in-chief on Thursday, because on Thursday we have limited time only. Thank you for this. And goodbye, enjoy the rest of the day in Banja Luka. Thank you. This concludes the videohearing. The trial stays adjourned until a quarter to 5.00. [The witness's testimony via videolink concluded]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I apologise for this delay, but extremely urgent matters had to be resolved immediately. I didn't conclude today's hearing immediately after the videoconference in order to have some time in preparation of the next following days. Let us first for a moment please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
